hero.title: Databases & SQL — Talking to Data
hero.hook: Every time you search something online, buy something from an app, or check your bank balance — a database is working. Databases store, organise and retrieve billions of records in milliseconds. SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you talk to these databases. And in Class 12 CS boards, SQL queries are worth 10–12 marks — the highest single topic in the exam.

hook_section.scenario: Your school keeps student data: name, class, marks, attendance, fees. You want to find all students in Class 12 with marks above 80. Without SQL, you'd read thousands of records manually. With SQL: SELECT name FROM students WHERE class=12 AND marks>80; — one line, instant result. That's the power of SQL.
hook_section.bridge: Chapter 3 covers RDBMS concepts (tables, keys, relations), SQL commands (DDL: CREATE/DROP/ALTER; DML: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE; DCL: GRANT/REVOKE), aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MAX, MIN), GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, and JOIN operations. SQL queries are always tested in the exam.
hook_section.punchline: SQL has four question types in boards: SELECT with conditions (WHERE), aggregate functions (GROUP BY/HAVING), ORDER BY, and table operations (CREATE/INSERT/UPDATE). Master these four.

concept_section.analogy: A database is like a school register — a table with rows (records = individual students) and columns (fields = name, roll no, marks). SQL is the language of instructions you give to the register keeper. SELECT = tell me specific rows/columns. WHERE = only if certain condition is true. GROUP BY = organise by category and calculate totals. JOIN = combine two registers.
concept_section.principle: SELECT col FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY col GROUP BY col HAVING condition. DDL: CREATE TABLE t (col datatype), ALTER, DROP. DML: INSERT INTO, UPDATE SET WHERE, DELETE WHERE. Keys: Primary (unique identifier), Foreign (links tables), Candidate (potential primary).

reveals.answer:
SELECT Name, Marks FROM Student ORDER BY Marks DESC;  -- highest first
SELECT Name FROM Student ORDER BY Name ASC;  -- alphabetical
SELECT DISTINCT City FROM Customer;  -- removes duplicates
SELECT TOP 3 Name FROM Student ORDER BY Marks DESC;  -- top 3 (MySQL: LIMIT 3)

reveals.question: 🔑 DDL and DML commands?

points: SELECT...FROM...WHERE: core query structure; WHERE filters rows
Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN — work on column values
GROUP BY: groups rows; HAVING: filters groups (after grouping, like WHERE for groups)
Primary Key: unique, not null; Foreign Key: links two tables

exam_questions.question: Given table Employee(EmpID, Name, Dept, Salary, City). Write SQL to: (a) Display all employees in 'IT' department earning more than 50000. (b) Find average salary department-wise. (c) Display names in alphabetical order. (d) Count total employees.
What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING clause in SQL?
What is a Primary Key? Give an example.

quiz.q: To display only unique values of City column, use:
quiz.exp: SELECT DISTINCT City FROM TableName removes duplicate city names and shows each city only once. DISTINCT is a keyword that eliminates duplicate values from results.

HAVING works with GROUP BY to filter groups based on aggregate conditions. Example: GROUP BY Dept HAVING AVG(Salary)>50000. WHERE filters individual rows (before grouping); HAVING filters groups (after grouping).

quiz.q: To find the second highest salary, the SQL approach is:
quiz.exp: SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employee). This subquery first finds the maximum, then finds the maximum of salaries below that value = second highest.

opts: All rows but keeps the table structure
quiz.exp: DELETE FROM Student (without WHERE) deletes ALL rows/records but keeps the table structure intact. DROP TABLE Student removes the entire table including structure. TRUNCATE also removes all rows faster.

flipcards.front: SQL query to find average marks of Class XII students?
flipcards.back: SELECT AVG(Marks) FROM Student WHERE Class='XII';
WHERE: filters rows BEFORE grouping. HAVING: filters groups AFTER GROUP BY. Can't use aggregate functions in WHERE.
Pattern matching: % = any sequence of characters. 'A%' = starts with A. '%a%' = contains 'a'. '_a' = any single char followed by 'a'.
A column that references the Primary Key of another table — creates a relationship between two tables

flipcards.front: SQL to increase all salaries by 10%?

flipcards.back: Sort by Marks column in descending order (highest first). ASC = ascending (lowest first, also the default)
